column2: Do I need a written employment contract?. Contracts & engagement. The Fair Work Act does not mandate a written contract for most ongoing employees, but one is effectively required to properly engage casuals, fixed-term staff, and anyone on an Individual Flexibility Arrangement. Whatever is agreed, it cannot undercut the NES or the applicable modern award — any such term is void and the statutory minimum applies instead. Common questions: Do I need to give him something in writing or is a handshake fine? Can I just use the contract I found on Google? What actually has to be in an employment letter? Is my old contract template still legal?

Fixed-term contract limits (2-yr cap, one renewal, FTCIS). Contracts & engagement. Since 6 December 2023, fixed-term contracts generally cannot exceed 2 years (including renewals), cannot be renewed more than once, and cannot include an "evergreen" auto-renewal clause, subject to a list of exceptions (e.g., genuine seasonal work, specific-task funding, high-income employees). Employers must give a Fixed Term Contract Information Statement (FTCIS) each time they enter a new fixed-term contract. Common questions: Can I just keep rolling her 12-month contract every year? What's this Fixed Term Contract Information Statement I keep hearing about? Is a 3-year fixed contract even legal now? She's on her second 1-year contract — am I in trouble?

Employee vs contractor - new "whole of relationship" test. Classification. From 26 August 2024, a new s15AA of the Fair Work Act requires the "real substance, practical reality and true nature" of the relationship to be assessed — looking at the totality of the relationship including how the contract is actually performed in practice, not just the contract's wording. This overturns the High Court's 2022 contract-first approach (*Personnel Contracting*/*Jamsek*) for Fair Work Act purposes, reintroducing the pre-2022 multi-factor test. Common questions: I've got a contractor who's basically been here 3 years working like an employee — am I okay? Does having an ABN and invoicing make someone a contractor? What actually decides if someone's an employee or a contractor now? My accountant says he's a contractor but I'm not sure that's still right

Sham contracting. Classification. Sham contracting occurs when an employer deliberately (or recklessly) misrepresents an employment relationship as an independent contracting arrangement, typically to avoid award/NES/super obligations. It is a distinct, separately penalised contravention from simple misclassification. Common questions: Could I get done for sham contracting even if I didn't mean to? I genuinely thought he was a contractor — is that a defence? What's the actual fine for getting this wrong? Are labour-hire and 'contractor' the same risk?

Contractor high-income threshold & opt-out notice. Classification. A contractor earning above the "contractor high income threshold" ($190,100 for the year starting 1 July 2026) can give a written opt-out notice electing not to be assessed under the new whole-of-relationship test, preserving contractor status even if the relationship otherwise looks employee-like. The notice can be revoked once. Common questions: He earns good money, does that mean he's automatically a contractor? What's this opt-out notice thing my contractor mentioned? Can a contractor change their mind after opting out? Does the threshold change every year?

Casual employment - new statutory definition. Classification. Since 26 August 2024, a person is a casual employee only if there is "no firm advance commitment to continuing and indefinite work," assessed on the real substance and practical reality of the relationship (not just contract wording). Casuals are paid a loading (commonly 25%) in lieu of paid leave and other permanent entitlements. Common questions: She's worked the same 3 shifts a week for 2 years — is she still legally casual? What actually makes someone a 'real' casual now? Can I lose the casual loading argument if this goes to Fair Work? Do I need to change her to permanent myself, or does she have to ask?

Casual conversion - Employee Choice Pathway. Classification. Replacing the old employer-initiated casual conversion regime, the Employee Choice Pathway (from 26 February 2025, or 26 August 2025 for small employers under 15 employees) lets casual employees themselves initiate a move to permanent employment once they've been employed 6 months (12 months for small business) and believe they no longer meet the casual definition. Common questions: One of my casuals wants to go permanent — what do I actually have to do? Can I say no if I don't want to make her permanent? How long do I have to respond to a conversion request? Is this different for small businesses like mine?

Which award (if any) applies. Award coverage. Over 120 modern awards exist, each with a coverage clause (typically clause 4) defining which industries/occupations it applies to. An employer is covered if the business falls within the award's defined industry; an employee is covered if a matching classification exists for their role. Awards cannot be contracted out of. Common questions: Which award actually covers my business? I run a café that also does catering — which award wins? Do I even need to worry about an award if I pay above minimum wage? My employee's title doesn't match anything in the award — now what?

Getting the classification level right. Award coverage. Once the correct award is identified, each award contains multiple classification levels tied to skill, qualifications, and duties, which determine the minimum pay rate. The Commission assesses this by the "principal purpose" for which the employee was employed, not simply their job title. Common questions: What level is a 'store supervisor' under this award? She's basically doing a level 4 job but I'm paying her level 2 — is that a problem? How do I know which classification my employee actually falls under? Do quals or experience decide the level?

Correct base pay rates & keeping up with wage rises. Pay. Award minimum rates change with the Fair Work Commission's Annual Wage Review (effective 1 July each year) and periodic award-specific variations. Employers must apply the correct current rate for the employee's classification, award, employment type (casual loading) and any applicable increment. Common questions: Did the minimum wage go up again this year? How do I know if I'm still paying above award? My payroll software says the rate changed — is that right? What's the new rate for my award as of July?

Penalty rates, overtime & allowances. Pay. Most awards layer penalty rates (weekends, public holidays, evenings/nights), overtime, and allowances (uniform, tool, travel, meal, first aid, etc.) on top of the base rate, each with its own trigger conditions. These are the entitlements most frequently missed in payroll builds. Common questions: Do I have to pay extra for Sunday shifts? What allowances am I supposed to be paying on top of wages? Is overtime automatic after 38 hours or does it depend on the roster? He worked on a public holiday — what do I owe him?

Annualised salary arrangements & reconciliation. Pay. Many awards (e.g. Clerks Private Sector, Manufacturing, Banking/Finance/Insurance) have specific annualised wage clauses — in force since 1 March 2020 — requiring employers to record the components the salary is meant to cover, set an "outer limit" of hours/penalties absorbed, and conduct an annual (or more frequent) reconciliation, topping up any shortfall. Common questions: I pay her a good salary — does that cover all the extra award stuff automatically? Do I have to do a formal reconciliation every year or is that overkill for a small team? What's an 'outer limit' clause and do I need one? If the salary falls short one year, what do I actually have to do?

The NES as the compliance floor. NES/leave. The NES is a set of minimum entitlements (maximum weekly hours, flexible work requests, parental leave, various paid/unpaid leave types, public holidays, notice/redundancy pay, casual conversion rights, and the Fair Work Information Statement) that apply to every national-system employee regardless of award, agreement or contract terms. Common questions: What am I legally required to give every employee, no matter what? Is this an award thing or a national law thing? Do casuals get all the same NES rights as everyone else? What's actually in the NES — is there a checklist?

Annual leave - accrual, excess, cashing out. NES/leave. Full-time employees accrue 4 weeks' paid annual leave per year (5 for some shiftworkers), accruing progressively and carrying over indefinitely if unused. Awards may permit "excess leave" direction (requiring an employee to take leave when their balance grows too large) and cashing out of a portion of accrued leave under strict conditions. Common questions: He's sitting on 8 weeks of annual leave — can I make him take some? Can I just pay out unused leave instead of her taking it? How much leave does a part-timer accrue? Does annual leave expire if it's not used?

Personal/carer's leave & the casual gap. NES/leave. Non-casual employees accrue 10 days' paid personal/carer's leave per year of service, accruing progressively and carrying over (unlike annual leave, unused personal leave does not usually get paid out on termination). Casuals are not entitled to paid personal leave but do get 2 days' unpaid carer's leave per occasion. Common questions: How many sick days does everyone get? Can I ask for a medical certificate every time? Does a casual get paid sick leave? What's the difference between sick leave and carer's leave — are they the same bucket?

Parental leave & the govt PPL interaction. NES/leave. The NES gives eligible employees up to 12 months' unpaid parental leave (with a right to request a further 12 months), separate from the Commonwealth Paid Parental Leave (PPL) scheme administered by Services Australia, which is expanding to 130 days (26 weeks) for children born/adopted from 1 July 2026, now with an employer-independent 12% government superannuation contribution (PPLSC) starting to flow from July 2026. Common questions: Do I have to pay her while she's on maternity leave? How does government paid parental leave actually work — do I administer it? Does she still get super while she's on parental leave now? How long can someone be away and still have a job to come back to?

Long service leave - state-by-state. NES/leave. Long service leave (LSL) is not part of the NES — it is governed separately by each state/territory. NSW, QLD, WA and TAS give 8.6667 weeks at 10 years' service; VIC and ACT give 6.0667 weeks at 7 years; SA and NT give 13 weeks at 10 years. Pro-rata access rules on early termination also differ significantly by state (e.g. NSW allows pro-rata after 5 years for most termination reasons; QLD's pro-rata trigger is narrower and tied to specified termination reasons). Common questions: How much long service leave does someone get after 10 years? Is long service leave different in each state? If I make someone redundant after 6 years, do they get any long service leave payout? We're based in NSW but have a remote worker in Queensland — whose LSL rules apply?

Compassionate/bereavement leave (incl. miscarriage). NES/leave. All employees, including casuals, get 2 days' compassionate leave per permissible occasion (paid for permanent staff, unpaid for casuals) on the death, life-threatening illness/injury of an immediate family/household member, a stillbirth, or a miscarriage. The Sex Discrimination and Fair Work (Respect at Work) Amendment Act 2021 extended coverage explicitly to miscarriage (loss before 20 weeks), for either partner, regardless of how the pregnancy was achieved. Common questions: Does compassionate leave cover a miscarriage? Do casuals get bereavement leave too? How many days off does someone get when a family member dies? Is this the same as 'bereavement leave' or something different?

Paid family & domestic violence leave. NES/leave. All employees, including casuals, are entitled to 10 days' paid family and domestic violence (FDV) leave in a 12-month period, available upfront (not accrued progressively) and non-cumulative year to year. Small businesses (fewer than 15 employees) had a delayed commencement (1 August 2023) compared to larger employers (1 February 2023). Common questions: How do I record this on the payslip without outing what it's for? Does my casual staff member get this leave too? Does it roll over if she doesn't use it this year? What evidence can I ask for?

Community service leave (jury/emergency). NES/leave. All employees, including casuals, can take unpaid community service leave for voluntary emergency management activities (SES, CFA, RSPCA rescue, etc.) with no cap on duration. Jury duty is a distinct sub-category where non-casual employees are entitled to "make-up pay" — the difference between their base rate and any court jury payment — for the first 10 days. Common questions: Do I have to pay him while he's on jury duty? She's a volunteer firefighter and got called out — what do I owe her? Is there a limit on how much time off for jury duty or emergency service? Do casuals get this too?

Record-keeping obligations. Payroll. Employers must keep specific employment records (pay, hours, leave, superannuation contributions, and more) for 7 years after an employee's termination, in English, legible, accurate, and readily accessible, with any correction clearly noted. Common questions: How long do I legally have to keep old payroll records? What actually has to be in an employee file? I don't have proper records for an ex-employee from years ago — how much trouble am I in? Can I just use a spreadsheet or does it need to be 'official'?

Pay slip compliance. Payroll. Pay slips must be issued within one working day of pay day and must include specific mandated content: employer name and ABN, employee name, pay period, payment date, gross and net amounts, any separately identifiable entitlements (bonus, loading, allowance, penalty rate, overtime), and superannuation fund/account details for any contribution made. Common questions: What actually has to be on a payslip? Is it okay to just show one lump sum or do I need to break it down? How quickly do payslips have to go out after payday? Do I need to show super on the payslip even if I haven't paid it yet this quarter?

Timesheet accuracy feeding award interpretation. Payroll. Accurate time and attendance capture is the practical foundation on which correct award interpretation, penalty rates, overtime, and superannuation calculation all depend — award pay outcomes are only as reliable as the underlying hours data. Common questions: Do I actually need timesheets if I trust my staff? How accurate do my records need to be? What happens if my roster and actual hours worked don't match? Can I estimate hours or does it need to be exact?

Super guarantee - rate, OTE, timing. Payroll/super. The Superannuation Guarantee (SG) rate reached its final legislated level of 12% from 1 July 2025 (no further scheduled increases). Employers must correctly calculate SG on Ordinary Time Earnings (OTE — not always the same as gross pay; excludes overtime in most cases but includes many allowances) and pay it to the correct fund on time. Common questions: Is super still going up, or did it stop at 12%? Do I pay super on overtime? What counts as 'ordinary time earnings' for super purposes? Do casuals get super too?

Payday Super (biggest 2026 payroll change). Payroll/super. From 1 July 2026, employers must pay super at the same time as wages (within a short window of each payday) rather than quarterly, moving to "Qualifying Earnings" as the calculation base and an annual (rather than quarterly) maximum contribution base. Late/short payments will trigger a revised, more immediate SGC exposure. Common questions: Do I really have to pay super every single payday now? What's 'Qualifying Earnings' — is that different to what I calculate now? How much time do I actually have after payday to get the super in? What happens if I'm late under the new system — is it worse than before?

Underpayment / wage-theft criminal offence + voluntary Code. Payroll/compliance. From 1 January 2025, intentional underpayment of wages/entitlements is a criminal offence (not honest mistakes), carrying penalties up to $7.825 million for companies and up to 10 years' imprisonment for individuals. The Voluntary Small Business Wage Compliance Code (also from 1 January 2025) gives businesses with fewer than 15 employees a framework that, if followed, means the FWO cannot refer them for criminal prosecution — civil remedies may still apply, since strict liability continues to govern correct payment of award/NES/agreement entitlements regardless of intent. Common questions: Could I go to jail for a payroll mistake? What's this Wage Compliance Code everyone's talking about — do I need to sign up to something? Is an honest mistake treated the same as deliberate underpayment now? If I find I've underpaid someone, what should I do first?

Self-correcting a discovered underpayment. Payroll/compliance. Where an SME discovers it has underpaid staff (commonly through an award/classification review, a payroll system change, or an external audit), there is an expected process: calculate the full extent using correct historical rates and hours, back-pay promptly, and — depending on scale — consider self-reporting to the FWO, which can lead to a cooperation agreement taking criminal referral off the table. Common questions: I think I've been underpaying someone — what do I do now? How far back do I have to go to fix this? Should I tell Fair Work myself or just quietly fix it? How do I even calculate what I owe going back years?

Single Touch Payroll (STP) compliance. Payroll. STP requires employers to report payroll information (salary/wages, PAYG withholding, super) to the ATO each pay run through STP-enabled software, replacing end-of-year payment summaries with real-time reporting. Common questions: Do I have to use special software or can I keep using my spreadsheet? What actually gets reported to the ATO each pay run? What happens if I miss an STP report? Is STP the same thing as paying tax and super, or separate?

Probation / minimum-employment-period confusion. Onboarding/probation. Owners routinely believe "probation" is a legal status that lets them dismiss freely in the first 3–6 months. In reality, probation is a *contractual* concept with no standing in the Fair Work Act; the only statutory clock is the **minimum employment period (MEP)** — 6 months generally, or **12 months for small business employers (<15 staff)** — before unfair dismissal protections switch on. A new starter accrues full leave and other NES entitlements throughout probation regardless. Critically, general protections and discrimination claims have **no minimum employment period at all** — an employee can be dismissed on day one and still bring a claim. Common questions: They're still on probation, I can just let them go, right? We haven't hit six months yet so we're covered Do I need a reason if they're still in their trial period? Can I extend probation if I'm not sure yet? Is probation even a real thing here?

Weak/absent structured onboarding. Onboarding. SMEs frequently onboard with "here's your desk, ask Dave if you're stuck" rather than a structured 30/60/90-day plan with documented performance and behavioural expectations. Because expectations are never written down, the business has nothing to point to later if performance or conduct becomes an issue — which directly undermines any subsequent PIP, warning, or dismissal defence. Common questions: We just throw them in the deep end There's no real induction, you just pick it up as you go We never got around to a proper welcome pack Nobody told me what 'good' looked like in this role We do a first-day chat and that's about it

Which policies are mandatory vs advisable. Policies. No Australian law mandates an "employee handbook" as a document. But a cluster of *obligations* effectively force documentation: WHS laws require systems for hazard identification, consultation and incident response; the positive duty under the Sex Discrimination Act effectively requires an anti-harassment policy as evidence of "reasonable steps"; privacy law requires a privacy policy once staff/customer personal information is handled; awards and the NES require documented leave, rostering and pay processes. SMEs conflate "no law says I need a handbook" with "I don't need any policies," which is the trap. Common questions: Do I actually need a full handbook or just a contract? We downloaded a template years ago, is it still legit? What's the bare minimum I need to not get caught out? Our policy folder hasn't been touched since we started Is a verbal 'we don't tolerate that' enough?

No feedback / no documentation trail. Performance. SME managers, often promoted for technical skill not people skill, avoid direct feedback conversations and let issues fester until they become a crisis, then want to move straight to dismissal. Because nothing was ever raised or documented, the eventual dismissal looks — and legally is — procedurally unfair, since Fair Work Commission unfair dismissal criteria explicitly weigh whether the employee was notified of the reason and given a chance to respond before any action. Common questions: I've mentioned it to them a few times, does that count as a warning? I don't want to make it awkward, we're a small team Can I just let them go, everyone knows they're not pulling their weight We've never actually put anything in writing I've been too nice for too long

Designing & running a defensible PIP. Performance. A Performance Improvement Plan is not itself a legal requirement, but where used it must be procedurally fair: specific deficiencies, clear and realistic standards, genuine support/resources, a reasonable timeframe, and a clear (and honestly communicated) consequence if targets aren't met. A dismissal following a PIP that was set up to fail, was unrealistic, or offered no real support is a significant unfair dismissal risk in its own right — the Commission scrutinises the *process*, not just the outcome. Common questions: We put them on a PIP but I think we've already made up our mind How long do we legally have to give them? What happens if they say they were never really supported? Do we need a written warning before the PIP or does the PIP count as the warning? They passed the PIP on paper but we still don't think they're right for the role

Progressive discipline & procedural fairness. Discipline. Standard Australian practice is a graduated response — verbal warning, written warning, final written warning, then termination — proportionate to the issue, with each step requiring the employee be told the specific allegation, given a real chance to respond (commonly 24–48 hours' notice of any meeting), and allowed a support person. SMEs frequently short-circuit this either by escalating too fast for minor issues or by avoiding action altogether until it becomes serious misconduct. Common questions: Is a text message warning enough or does it need to be a letter? How many warnings do I actually need before I can let them go? Do I have to let them bring someone to the meeting? This is the third time, can I skip straight to a final warning? We've never had to do this before, where do I even start?

Serious misconduct / summary dismissal miscalls. Discipline. Summary (instant, no-notice) dismissal is legally available only where conduct is genuinely serious — theft, fraud, violence, or serious safety breaches are the Small Business Fair Dismissal Code's own examples — and even then the employer must have reasonable grounds, not just suspicion. SMEs frequently over-call "serious misconduct" for things that are really performance or minor conduct issues, skipping process entirely because they believe summary dismissal removes the need for warnings. Common questions: This is gross misconduct, I can sack them on the spot, right? Do I still need to pay them out if I fire them for this? I caught them doing X, can I march them out today? Is swearing at a customer enough to skip the warnings?

Unfair dismissal & Small Business Fair Dismissal Code. Termination. Unfair dismissal is the single largest category of Fair Work Commission lodgment — **37% of all applications in both 2023–24 and 2024–25**, with FWC receiving 44,075 total lodgments in 2024–25 and an **11% year-on-year increase** in unfair dismissal applications. For a small business employer (<15 employees), compliance with the **Small Business Fair Dismissal Code is a complete defence** if followed — but the Code still requires a valid reason and (for performance) a prior warning; it is not a free pass to dismiss without process, a very common misconception. Common questions: We're under 15 people so we're covered, aren't we? Can they even take us to Fair Work if we followed the Code? It's cheaper to just pay them out than fight it Filing a claim only costs them like $90, so everyone does it We got a conciliation notice out of nowhere

General protections / adverse action. Termination. General protections (adverse action) claims are structurally more dangerous than unfair dismissal for SMEs because there is **no minimum employment period, no small-business exemption, no compensation cap, and courts can add penalties on top of compensation**. Performance management itself is repeatedly flagged as a "flashpoint": if an employee has recently exercised a workplace right (raised a safety issue, requested leave, made a complaint) and is then warned, performance-managed, or dismissed, the *timing alone* can support a claim regardless of whether the underlying performance issue was genuine — the onus shifts to the employer to prove the workplace right was **not** a reason for the action. Common questions: They only complained after we started managing their performance How do we prove we weren't punishing them for that? There's no cap on what we could have to pay? This feels like it could snowball into something huge We didn't even know raising it was a 'workplace right'

Redundancy - genuine test & small-business exemption. Termination. Small business employers (<15 employees) are **exempt from statutory redundancy pay** under the NES — but this exemption has real limits: it doesn't override redundancy clauses in an applicable award, enterprise agreement, or the employment contract itself, and notice (or pay in lieu) is still owed regardless. Separately, to be a *genuine* redundancy at all (protecting against an unfair dismissal claim), the employer must show the role is genuinely no longer needed, consultation obligations (where an award/agreement applies) were met, and redeployment was considered. Common questions: We're under 15 staff so we don't have to pay redundancy, do we? Is 'restructuring' enough of a reason on its own? Do I need to consult if it's just one role going? Their contract mentions redundancy pay, does that override the exemption? Can I make the role redundant and then just hire someone else to do it?

Notice periods & final pay errors. Termination. NES minimum notice scales with continuous service (up to 4 weeks, plus an extra week for employees over 45 with 2+ years' service), and casuals are not entitled to notice. Awards or contracts can require longer notice than the NES minimum. SMEs frequently get final pay wrong — miscalculating notice-in-lieu, missing accrued leave entitlements, or applying the wrong notice period for tenure — which converts an otherwise clean termination into an underpayment dispute layered on top of any dismissal claim. Common questions: How much notice do we actually owe them? Do we pay out their notice or have them work it? What do we owe on top of notice, just leave? They've been here two years, is that different to someone at six months?

Flexible working arrangement requests. Flexible work. Eligible employees (e.g. parents, carers, over 55, experiencing family/domestic violence, or with a disability) have a statutory right under s.65 of the Fair Work Act to request flexible working arrangements, and employers must respond in writing within **21 days**, can only refuse on **genuine reasonable business grounds**, and — critically — must first **discuss the request and genuinely try to reach agreement** on alternatives before refusing. The Fair Work Commission now has expanded powers to arbitrate disputes about these refusals. Common questions: We're too small to do a four-day week, surely that's a valid reason Do I have to put the refusal in writing or can I just tell them? What counts as a 'genuine' business ground? They want to work from home permanently, can I just say no? Now Fair Work can actually rule on this?

Right to Disconnect in daily practice. Flexible work. The right to disconnect gives employees the right to refuse to monitor, read or respond to work contact outside working hours **unless that refusal is unreasonable**, weighed against factors like the reason for contact, how it's made, and the employee's role/circumstances. It commenced for large employers in **August 2024** and for **small business employers (<15 employees) on 26 August 2025** — meaning as at August 2026 it has been live for small business for exactly one year and is now a live, current obligation, not a future one. Common questions: Can I even text them about tomorrow's shift after hours? Does this apply to us now, we're small? What counts as 'unreasonable' to expect a reply? We've always just called if something came up, are we breaking the law now? Do we need a written policy on this or just a chat?

Managing psychosocial hazards (new Code). WHS. Since 2022–2024 (varying by state, with the model Code finalised and Commonwealth version registered as a legislative instrument), WHS duty-holders must manage **psychosocial hazards** — poor workplace relationships/behaviours, high job demands, low job control, poor support, role ambiguity, remote/isolated work, violence and bullying — with the **same rigour as physical hazards**: identify, assess, control, and review, so far as reasonably practicable. This is now a mainstream compliance obligation, not a "nice to have" wellbeing initiative. Common questions: We don't really have a WHS system, we're only five people Is stress actually something we're legally meant to manage now? What does a 'psychosocial risk assessment' even look like for us? We just deal with bullying complaints as they come up Do we need external help for this or can we DIY it?

Officer due diligence & right-sized WHS. WHS. Directors/owners who meet the "officer" definition have a **personal due diligence duty** — active verification that the business has and uses appropriate WHS processes, not passive trust that "someone's got it covered." For an SME this doesn't require a heavy compliance bureaucracy but does require documented basics: a simple safety policy, hazard/incident reporting process, emergency procedures, risk assessments for higher-risk tasks, and genuine (even informal) worker consultation. Common questions: I didn't realise that was on me personally, not just the business We don't have a full WHS system, is that going to be a problem? What's actually the bare minimum we need documented? Do I need to formally 'consult' or is chatting at smoko enough? Who's even responsible for this in a five-person company?

Defensible informal/low-level investigation. Conflict. Most SME "investigations" are informal — a bullying complaint, a clash between two staff, an allegation of unfair treatment — but still need a basically fair process: act promptly, document the complaint, interview complainant/accused/witnesses separately, give the accused details of the allegation and a chance to respond, weigh the evidence, and act on findings. Owners without HR training often either do nothing (fearing they'll make it worse) or act too fast on one side's account alone. Common questions: I don't know who's telling the truth here Do I need to formally 'investigate' this or can I just talk to them both? How do I stay impartial when I know them both personally? What do I actually need to write down? Someone's made a complaint, what happens now?

Retention & turnover. Culture. National turnover has actually fallen to a three-year low of **13.5% (June quarter 2026), down from 15.2% in December 2025** — an over-11% decline in six months — per AHRI's Quarterly Australian Work Outlook. Despite this, engagement is weak: Gallup's 2026 State of the Global Workplace put engagement at just **20%**, the lowest since 2020, with **managers identified as a major contributing factor**. The most cited reason employees leave is **excessive workload (26% of employers)**; the most-used retention levers are learning & development, flexible work, and wellbeing support (each cited by 36% of employers). Common questions: We just can't compete with the bigger players on pay Everyone's stretched too thin, that's why people leave We don't really do surveys, we just chat Losing one person here is like losing ten in a big company I don't know why they left, they just said 'it's not working out'

Managing absenteeism without a system. Culture. Absenteeism costs Australian employers an estimated **$33 billion a year** (presenteeism a further ~$35 billion), representing roughly **7–8% of total payroll** for most businesses, or **$4,000+ per employee per year**. Workers take **9–14 days of unplanned absence annually** depending on industry (hospitality highest at ~11.9 days), and a striking **52% of Australian workers admit to taking at least one "not really sick" sick day** (ELMO Q3 2025 sentiment survey). Mental health is an increasingly cited driver: more than half of employers reported increased mental-health-related absence in 2025. Common questions: They always seem to be sick on a Monday I don't want to be the bad guy but this keeps happening Is this actually a performance issue or a wellbeing issue? We can't just roster around someone who's out all the time Do I even have the right to ask why they're off?

Ad hoc training & key-person/succession risk. L&D. SMEs rarely have a training budget or framework; development happens informally ("learn on the job," occasional short course) and is the most-cited retention lever employers say they're leaning on (36%, per AHRI data above) despite having no structured process to deliver it. Succession risk compounds this: specialised knowledge often sits with one or two people, and losing them has a proportionally larger impact than in a large organisation — yet formal succession planning is rare below a certain size. Common questions: We don't really have a training budget, they just figure it out If Sarah left tomorrow we'd be in real trouble Succession planning feels like a big-company thing We can't afford to send people on courses Everything's in one person's head

Positive duty (Sex Discrimination Act) at SME scale. DEI/harassment. Since the positive duty commenced, **all employers — with no small-business exemption of any kind** — must take "reasonable and proportionate" steps to eliminate, as far as possible, sex-based harassment, sexual harassment, sex discrimination and related victimisation. The AHRC now has active inquiry and enforcement powers, has flagged **retail trade and accommodation/food services as high-risk priority industries**, and continues to update small-business-specific educational tools. "Reasonable and proportionate" is scaled to the size and resources of the business — meaning the *standard* flexes for an SME, but the *duty itself* does not disappear. Common questions: Surely this doesn't apply to a business our size What counts as 'reasonable steps' for five staff? We've never had a complaint so we're probably fine Do we need actual training or is a policy enough? Is this actually enforced against small businesses or just big ones?

Burnout & mental-health absence/presenteeism. Wellbeing. Around **half of Australian workers experienced burnout in the past year** (Beyond Blue, June 2025 national survey), and ELMO's Q3 2025 index found **40% experiencing burnout right now** (~4.3 million workers nationally). Younger workers (18–29) report the highest rates, driven by workload, lack of management support, and inflexible conditions. Despite this, only **5% accessed an Employee Assistance Program** in the same period — a 35-percentage-point gap between prevalence and help-seeking. The Productivity Commission estimates a **$2.30 return for every $1 invested** in workplace mental health, and up to **$18 billion/year** in benefits from recommended reforms nationally. Common questions: Everyone's just stretched thin, that's normal for a small business though, right? We can't afford an EAP I think they're burnt out but I don't know what to actually do about it Is this a performance issue or is something else going on? We don't really have a wellbeing policy as such

Whether to hire at all (backfill vs redesign vs automate). Workforce need. When a role becomes vacant (resignation, growth pressure, "we're drowning"), the SME owner/manager must decide whether to simply refill the same job, redesign it, split it across existing staff, outsource/automate it, or use temporary/contract cover while deciding. Without an HR function, this decision is usually made reactively and fast, under operational pressure. Common questions: Do I actually need to replace her or can we just restructure? We're drowning, I need someone yesterday. Can I get away with not backfilling this one? Should this be a full-time role or can I get a contractor/temp to cover it for now? Is this a hiring problem or a systems problem?

Choosing engagement type without misclassification risk. Workforce need. SMEs facing uncertain demand often default to "let's just get a contractor" or "make them casual for now" to preserve flexibility. Australian law treats this as a substance-over-form question: if the working relationship looks like employment (set hours, supervision, sole client, tools provided), the law will treat it as employment regardless of the label or ABN. Common questions: Can I just get them on an ABN to keep it simple? I don't want to commit to permanent yet, can we trial them as a contractor? What's the difference between casual and part-time for me as the employer? If I get this wrong, what actually happens to me?

Vague need -> accurate job description. Role design. The owner/manager knows the business is understaffed or a function is failing but struggles to translate "I need help" into a structured description of duties, required skills, reporting lines, and success measures. JDs are frequently copy-pasted from an old ad, a template found online, or a competitor's listing rather than built from actual task analysis. Common questions: I know what I need them to do, I just don't know how to write it up properly. Can you turn this into a proper position description for me? What do I even call this role? I've just copied our old ad from two years ago, is that still right?

Unicorn candidate / wishlist inflation. Role design. Hiring managers stack every desirable trait into one role (years of experience + multiple certifications + leadership history + specific software + culture fit) producing a spec that describes an idealised composite rather than a realistic hire. This is a job-design failure that surfaces at the ad-writing stage. Common questions: I want someone who can basically do everything I do. Ideally they'd have 10 years' experience but be happy on a junior wage. We need a unicorn, someone who ticks every box. Why isn't anyone applying who has ALL of this?

Role scope creep & level misalignment. Role design. The role as advertised/hired doesn't match the role as actually performed once the person starts — either because the JD undersold the true scope, or because the business keeps adding responsibilities post-hire ("job creep"). This creates downstream pay-band mismatch, retention risk, and disputes. Common questions: They've ended up doing way more than what we hired them for. Is this still the same job or has it basically turned into a different role? We keep adding stuff to their plate, should we be paying them more?

Job ad that attracts the right applicants. Job ads. SMEs need ads that filter for fit and reduce screening burden, but default to generic, template-driven ads (or, at the other extreme, ultra-vague ads) that attract high volumes of unsuitable applicants or too few of the right ones. Common questions: I posted the ad and got 200 applications and none of them are right. How do I make this ad sound good when we're a tiny business no one's heard of? I don't have time to read through all these CVs. What do I even put in a job ad? Can you just write it for me?

Avoiding discriminatory language/criteria in ads. Job ads. Ads must avoid direct or indirect discrimination on protected attributes (age, sex, disability, race, sexual orientation, gender identity, pregnancy, family/carer responsibilities, etc.) both in explicit wording ("under 30," "recent graduate only") and in disguised proxies (unnecessary experience thresholds, physical requirements not genuinely required for the job). Common questions: Can I say we're looking for someone young and energetic? Is it okay to ask for 'native English speaker'? We really want someone who's been in the industry a long time, is that discriminatory against younger people? Can I ask if they have kids, just so I know about their availability?

Right ad channel(s) & cost as an SME. Job ads. SMEs must pick between SEEK, Indeed, LinkedIn, niche/industry boards, social media, referral, or an agency — each with different cost structures, reach, and fit by role type — usually without any prior data on what has worked before. Common questions: Where should I even post this? Is SEEK worth the money or should I just use Indeed for free? Should I use a recruiter for this one or try to do it myself first? LinkedIn feels like it's for corporate roles, not us.

Credible EVP as a low-brand-recognition employer. EVP. SMEs must articulate why someone should work for them when they can't compete on brand recognition or, often, on headline salary — requiring them to identify and communicate genuine differentiators (flexibility, autonomy, growth, culture, purpose, job security in a stable local business). Common questions: Why would anyone want to work here over a bigger company? We can't compete on salary, what else have we got? Nobody's heard of us, how do I make the ad sound appealing? We're a great little team, I just don't know how to say that in an ad.

Ghost job perception & trust erosion. Job ads. Two related phenomena: (a) genuine employers' ads being mistaken for "ghost jobs" (roles with no real intent to hire, often posted for pipeline-building or to project growth) because candidates hear nothing back; (b) SME employers themselves losing time to candidates who apply speculatively or without real intent. Rising candidate distrust of job ads generally raises the bar for SME ads to look credible and prompt. Common questions: I haven't had time to get back to everyone who applied. People are saying we never responded, but we're just flat out. How do I know if the people applying are even serious? Is this job even still open? [candidate-side, illustrative]

Setting a defensible pay band without enterprise data. Pay banding. SMEs need to decide what to pay for a role but typically lack subscription access to enterprise compensation data (Mercer, PayScale, etc.) and instead rely on a patchwork of the relevant Modern Award, competitor job ads, recruiter conversations, and gut feel. Common questions: What should I actually be paying for this role? Am I overpaying/underpaying compared to everyone else? The award says one thing but everyone in my industry pays more, what do I do? How do I know if $X is fair for a regional area vs the city?

Whether/how to advertise salary (transparency). Pay banding. Whether to publish a salary range in the job ad, and if so, how (fixed figure vs range vs "circa"), is now a live decision for every SME ad, driven by candidate expectation shift and by SEEK's own product-level nudges toward disclosure. Common questions: Do I really have to put the salary in the ad? If I put a number, will my current staff find out and want more? I don't want people just applying for the money. Competitive salary" is easier to write than a number." [illustrative reasoning, not a literal quote]

Avoiding illegal/underpaid job-ad rates (FWO). Pay banding/compliance. It is a specific, enforceable offence in Australia to advertise a job at a pay rate below the applicable minimum entitlement under an Award, enterprise agreement, or the National Minimum Wage. This is distinct from D1/D2 — it is a hard compliance floor, not a competitiveness question. Common questions: I didn't realise the award had gone up. We've always paid this rate, I didn't know it wasn't enough anymore. What award even covers this role? Can I offer a flat rate that covers penalties, or do I have to itemise it?

Gender pay equity exposure below WGEA threshold. Pay banding. Formal WGEA gender-pay-gap public reporting only applies to employers with 100+ employees (covering roughly 5,000–8,500 employers nationally), meaning the overwhelming majority of Australian SMEs are not required to report. However, the underlying legal obligation — equal remuneration for work of equal or comparable value under the Fair Work Act — applies regardless of employer size, and reputational/candidate-facing pay-equity expectations increasingly flow down to SMEs regardless of the reporting threshold. Common questions: We're way under 100 staff, so this doesn't apply to us, right? I just pay people what I negotiated with them individually, is that a problem? Do I need to worry about pay equity if we're small?

Salary negotiation & counter-offers. Pay banding. Once candidates engage, SMEs must handle negotiation above the advertised figure (or above the owner's internal expectation), and increasingly must respond to competing counter-offers from a candidate's current employer trying to retain them. Common questions: They're asking for more than we advertised, can we move? Their current employer counter-offered, now what? If I go up for this person, will everyone else expect the same? How much wiggle room should I actually build into the number I put in the ad?

Reading a bifurcated market. Sourcing. SMEs need to calibrate expectations to the specific occupation and region they're hiring into, not the aggregate national narrative. Aggregate indicators (more applications per ad, longer hiring timelines, softer ad volumes) suggest an easing, employer-favourable shift, but this masks acute, persistent shortages in health, trades, and some professional/technical occupations. Common questions: Everyone says it's easier to hire now, why am I still struggling to find a [tradesperson/nurse/technician]? I'm getting heaps of applications but none of them are qualified. Is now a good time to hire or should I wait? Why do I have to pay so much more than last year for the same role?

Employer-sponsored migration as an SME lever. Sourcing. With employer-sponsored permanent migration places increasing substantially for 2026–27 while overall net overseas migration is being deliberately reduced, the government's stated policy direction favours employer sponsorship as a shortage-filling pathway — but SMEs are typically the least likely business segment to know how to access it, given the cost, complexity, and lead time of sponsorship compared to larger employers with dedicated mobility/HR teams. Common questions: Could I sponsor someone from overseas for this role, and is it even worth the hassle for one person? What does it actually cost me to sponsor someone? I keep hearing there aren't enough [tradespeople/nurses] here, should I be looking overseas? How long does visa sponsorship actually take, I need someone soon.

Time-to-fill blowout & vacancy cost. Sourcing. While the national median time-to-fill sits around 32 days, this masks substantially longer fill times for niche, regional, or shortage-occupation SME vacancies — extending the operational and financial pain (overtime, lost revenue, burnout of remaining staff) that triggered the hire in the first place. Common questions: This role's been open for months and I still can't find anyone. We're all working overtime to cover the gap. I can't afford to wait for the 'perfect' person any more, I just need someone. How long is this actually going to take?

Resume overload with no triage system. Screening. Easy-apply job boards and AI-written applications mean an SME advertising one role can receive hundreds of applications, most of them low-fit. The owner/manager doing hiring alongside their day job has no formal way to triage volume, so screening either takes days (delaying time-to-hire) or gets rushed and superficial. Common questions: the pile just keeps growing," "I'm drowning in applications," "half of these aren't even close," "I just skim for keywords," "I don't have time to read 200 CVs," "we ghost most of them because who has time to reply.

AI-assisted resume screening & algorithmic bias. Screening. SMEs increasingly buy ATS/screening tools with AI ranking features to cope with volume (A1). These tools learn from historical hiring patterns and can reproduce and amplify bias — screening out candidates based on proxies for race, disability, age or gender (non-Anglo names, employment gaps, postcode, graduation year) rather than job-relevant criteria. Common questions: the software just ranks them for me," "I don't really know how it scores," "it filters out the ones without the right keywords," "the vendor said it's bias-free," "black box," "I just trust the shortlist it gives me.

No consistent CV scoring rubric. Screening. Screening decisions in most SMEs are made against an informal mental checklist rather than a written, weighted rubric applied consistently to every applicant. This produces inconsistent, hard-to-defend outcomes and makes it difficult to demonstrate merit-based selection if challenged. Common questions: I just know it when I see it," "gut feel," "does this person feel right," "we don't really score, we just talk about it," "gone with my instinct.

Undocumented, indefensible shortlisting. Shortlisting. Shortlisting is where the applicant pool is cut to interview-stage, and it is the point at which discrimination complaints most often crystallise ("why was I not even interviewed?"). Many SMEs shortlist informally — a quick read-through and a verbal "let's talk to these three" — with no written rationale for who was cut and why. Common questions: we had a chat and picked our top three," "I could just tell from the CV," "didn't feel like a culture fit," "not what we're looking for" (used without a stated reason), "we'll just go with our shortlist.

Inconsistent, unstructured phone screens. Phone/video screen. Initial phone screens in SMEs are typically freeform 10-15 minute chats rather than a structured set of questions applied to every candidate. This makes it hard to compare candidates objectively and increases the risk that unconscious bias, rapport, or unlawful topics (family status, age, health) creep into the conversation. Common questions: just a quick chat to see if they're keen," "suss them out," "gauge their vibe," "quick sense check before we bring them in," "weed out the time-wasters.

One-way AI video interviews - backlash & legal footing. Phone/video screen. Some SMEs (often via a recruitment agency or platform) now use one-way, asynchronous video interviews where candidates record themselves answering set questions, sometimes with AI-generated scoring of tone, word choice or facial expression. Candidates report finding these impersonal and are increasingly wary of how the recording and any biometric-adjacent data (face, voice) is used, stored and possibly used to train vendor models. Common questions: record yourself answering these three questions," "the AI gives us a score out of 100," "candidates hate these," "feels like talking to a wall," "creepy," "no idea what happens to the video after.

Unlawful / discriminatory interview questions. Interview design. Hiring managers without HR training routinely ask questions that are unlawful or high-risk under Australian anti-discrimination law — about age, marital/family status, pregnancy plans, health, religion, or country of origin — usually with no discriminatory intent, simply trying to "get to know" the candidate or assess availability/reliability. Common questions: just wanted to know if she's planning a family," "asked if he could handle the physical side of the job," "wanted to make sure they could work weekends so asked about kids," "just making conversation," "didn't think it was a big deal.

Unstructured, gut-feel interviewing. Interview design. Most SME interviews are conversational and unstructured: different questions for different candidates, no fixed rubric, decisions driven by rapport and first impressions rather than evidence against job-relevant criteria. This is the single biggest driver of both poor hiring decisions and legal exposure in the interview stage. Common questions: I just go with my gut," "you know within the first five minutes," "we just have a chat," "didn't feel right," "loved their energy," "not sure why, just a vibe thing.

Interview scorecard design & panel calibration. Interview design. Where SMEs do use interview scorecards, they're often poorly designed (too many vague criteria, no anchored rating scale) and, in panel interviews, scored via open group discussion rather than independent scoring followed by calibration — which allows the first or most senior voice to anchor everyone else's assessment. Common questions: we all just talked it through," "the boss decides anyway," "we compare notes after," "everyone kind of agreed," "went with the room.

Disproportionate/irrelevant psychometric testing. Assessments. SMEs sometimes apply generic personality or cognitive tests to every role regardless of relevance, either because a recruitment platform bundles them in by default or because a manager believes more testing equals more rigour. Used disproportionately, this adds cost, slows time-to-hire, and can introduce discrimination risk if the test isn't validated for the role or disadvantages particular groups. Common questions: we run everyone through a personality test," "it gives us a fit score," "makes the process feel more scientific," "not sure what the numbers actually mean, but it feels thorough," "the software recommended it.

Reasonable adjustments in assessments (disability). Assessments. Where skills tests, timed assessments or interviews aren't adapted for candidates with disability, SMEs risk both excluding capable candidates and breaching the Disability Discrimination Act 1992. Reasonable adjustment could mean extra time, an alternative format, or a different assessment method altogether that still measures the same job-relevant capability. Common questions: didn't know we had to do that," "we just run the standard test for everyone," "didn't want to single anyone out," "they didn't mention anything so we assumed it was fine.

Reference checks - legal risk & low value. Checks. Reference checking remains near-universal practice but is often done inconsistently (different questions per candidate, unstructured notes) and both sides are cautious about what they say — candidates supply hand-picked referees and employers/referees fear defamation or negligent-referral exposure, so reference calls often yield little beyond confirming dates of employment. Common questions: just a box-ticking call," "they'll only give you their best mate as a referee anyway," "HR won't say anything beyond dates and title now," "hard to get anyone to say anything real," "read between the lines.

Police/criminal checks as an overreaching filter. Checks. Some SMEs require a national police check for every role regardless of relevance, and treat any disclosed record as an automatic disqualifier ("any record = no job"), rather than assessing whether the specific offence is relevant to the specific role's inherent requirements. Common questions: we run a police check on everyone as standard," "any record and it's a no from us," "just our policy," "can't risk it," "better safe than sorry.

Right-to-work / visa verification (VEVO) gaps. Checks. Employers are legally required to verify a prospective employee's right to work in Australia before employment starts, and to monitor visa conditions (expiry, work-hour limits, sponsorship conditions) for the duration of employment. VEVO (Visa Entitlement Verification Online), run by the Department of Home Affairs, is the mechanism for this — it confirms visa status, work rights, conditions and expiry with the visa holder's consent. Many SMEs either skip this check, do it only at the start (not on an ongoing basis for time-limited visas), or rely on candidate self-report without verification. Common questions: took their word for it," "didn't think to check," "assumed the agency handled that," "we'll sort the visa stuff once they start," "PR, so didn't need to check" (often stated without verification).

Qualification/credential verification gaps. Checks. Employers frequently accept a copy of a degree, diploma or trade certificate at face value without independent verification, creating exposure to CV fraud. Documented Australian cases include organised operations selling fake degree/diploma certificates purportedly from dozens of real TAFEs and universities, and fraudulent trade certificate schemes issuing false construction industry qualifications. Common questions: took the certificate at face value," "looked legit to me," "didn't think to call the uni," "we usually only check for the licensed roles," "sighted the original, that's usually enough for us.

Offer letters/contracts missing essential terms. Offer. SME offer letters are frequently informal (a short email confirming a start date and salary) and miss essential terms that protect both parties — employment type, ordinary hours, location, superannuation, probation terms and notice provisions, and reference to the Fair Work Information Statement. This creates ambiguity that surfaces later as a dispute. Common questions: just sent a quick email confirming the details," "we'll sort the formal contract later," "verbal offer first, paperwork to follow," "kept it simple.

Probation period misunderstanding. Offer. SME employers frequently conflate the contractual probation period with the statutory minimum employment period for unfair dismissal protection (six months generally, 12 months for a small business employer with fewer than 15 employees), and mistakenly believe that dismissing someone "during probation" automatically shields them from all legal risk. Probation is a contractual concept the Fair Work Act does not define or require; general protections (adverse action) apply from day one regardless of probation status. Common questions: they're still on probation, so we can just let them go," "no risk while they're on their trial period," "haven't passed probation yet so it's fine," "three-month trial.

Counter-offers & lost candidates at the eleventh hour. Offer. SMEs frequently lose a preferred candidate at final-offer stage when the candidate's current employer counters to retain them — or the SME itself, needing to retain a departing staff member, makes an ultimately ineffective counter-offer. Evidence suggests counter-offers are a weak long-term retention fix in either direction. Common questions: they got counter-offered and pulled out," "lost them to their current employer at the last minute," "gutted, we thought it was locked in," "should have moved faster on the offer," "meeting salary expectations is our biggest headache.

Two-way candidate ghosting. Candidate experience. Ghosting now runs in both directions — candidates disappearing after applying or even after accepting an offer, and employers failing to respond to applicants at all (often the majority of a large applicant pool, per A1). Both damage the SME's ability to hire efficiently and its employer brand in a small, networked local labour market. Common questions: just stopped replying," "went dark," "no-showed the interview," "accepted then never turned up on day one," "we ghost most of them because who has time to reply," "radio silence.

Slow time-to-hire losing candidates. Candidate experience. SMEs without dedicated recruitment resourcing typically take longer to move from application to offer than larger, process-driven competitors, and lose strong candidates to faster-moving employers as a direct result — compounding the ghosting problem (H1) and the counter-offer problem (G3). Common questions: by the time we got back to them they'd taken another offer," "process just dragged on," "couldn't get everyone in the same room to decide," "took three weeks just to get to interview," "lost another good one to someone faster.

Cost-per-hire pressure & agency-fee dependency. Candidate experience. SMEs without in-house recruitment capability often default to recruitment agencies for anything beyond the simplest roles, paying placement fees typically in the range of 15-25% of the candidate's first-year salary — a significant cost relative to SME hiring budgets, especially when a placement doesn't work out and the process must be repeated. Common questions: the agency fee alone was more than we budgeted," "cheaper to do it ourselves but we don't have the time," "burned twice by a bad agency placement," "20% of salary just to find someone.

AI-driven hiring decisions & discrimination liability. AI-in-hiring. Australian anti-discrimination law (Racial Discrimination Act 1975, Sex Discrimination Act 1984, Age Discrimination Act 2004, Disability Discrimination Act 1992) and the Fair Work Act 2009's general protections apply in full to any hiring decision, regardless of whether a human or an algorithm made or informed it. There is no AI-specific exemption. Employers remain legally liable for discriminatory outcomes produced by a third-party AI tool, even where the discrimination is unintentional, statistically indirect (via a proxy such as postcode or graduation year), and even where the employer did not build or fully understand the tool. Common questions: the software just does the ranking," "the vendor says it's tested for bias," "didn't realise we were responsible for how it scores," "we just trust the shortlist," "it's a black box, honestly.

Privacy Act ADM transparency rule (from 10 Dec 2026). AI-in-hiring. Australia's Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) and the Australian Privacy Principles (APPs) apply to any AI recruitment tool that processes personal information (names, contact details, resumes, interview recordings, assessment results). A significant new obligation — Automated Decision-Making (ADM) transparency under new APP 1.7-1.9 — commences 10 December 2026, requiring organisations to update their privacy policies to disclose the kinds of personal information used in ADM and the kinds of decisions involved. Regulatory commentary explicitly identifies "deciding whether to give an applicant an interview" as likely falling within scope. Common questions: didn't know we needed a privacy policy update for that," "the software handles the data, not us, surely," "what does 'automated decision' even mean here," "we just use whatever the platform gives us.

Employee-records exemption uncertainty ("tranche two"). AI-in-hiring. Currently, s.7B(3) of the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) exempts private-sector employers from most Privacy Act obligations for acts and practices directly related to an existing employee's employment relationship — but this exemption does not cover job applicants/candidates, who are already fully protected. The exemption's future is itself uncertain: "tranche two" of Privacy Act reform, expected later in 2026, is actively considering narrowing or removing the employee-records exemption, alongside possible removal of the small-business exemption. As at 2026-08-10 these changes are proposed/under consultation, not law. Common questions: thought employee data was exempt anyway," "wasn't sure if that applied before they started," "heard the exemption might get scrapped," "waiting to see what happens with the reform before we build anything new.

No AI governance / vendor oversight in SME recruitment. AI-in-hiring. Even where SMEs are aware AI is embedded in their recruitment stack, few have any formal governance process — no policy on when AI-assisted decisions require human review, no record-keeping of AI-influenced outcomes, no process for periodically checking whether the tool's outputs look skewed across candidate groups. This is the practical gap sitting underneath both the discrimination risk (I1) and the privacy risk (I2): the law is clear that the employer is responsible, but most SMEs have no internal mechanism to discharge that responsibility. Common questions: we don't really have a policy on that," "just use it as it comes," "haven't looked into how it decides," "no one's really checking," "assumed the platform sorts that out.

Weak handoff from recruitment to onboarding. Onboarding handoff. In SMEs, the same person (owner/accidental HR rep) often runs recruitment and then onboarding, but without a formal handoff process — meaning compliance paperwork (TFN declaration, super choice form, Fair Work Information Statement), induction planning, and the transfer of candidate/interview information into the new starter's employee record are done ad hoc, late, or missed entirely. Early attrition is strongly linked to poor onboarding. Common questions: we'll sort the paperwork on day one," "kind of figure it out as we go," "didn't realise super forms weren't done until pay day," "the induction is basically just a chat and a tour," "wasn't really a formal handover, it's just me doing both.

HR tech gaps & "spreadsheet-and-hope" workflows. Tooling. Most Australian SMEs run people operations on a patchwork of spreadsheets, email threads, paper files, and whatever free tier their accounting software bundles in, rather than a purpose-built HR system. Employee files sit in scattered folders, leave requests live in inboxes, timesheets are separate spreadsheets, and none of it talks to payroll. The system only "works" because nothing has gone wrong yet — hence "spreadsheet-and-hope."

Record-keeping & documentary-evidence gaps. Tooling/compliance. Under s.535 of the Fair Work Act, employers must make and keep employee records for seven years covering pay, hours, leave, superannuation and more; specific documentation (the Small Business Fair Dismissal Code checklist, redundancy consultation records, performance-management file notes) is what actually determines whether an employer wins or loses a dispute. SMEs typically don't know the full list of what they're legally required to keep, and even when they do, they don't keep it consistently.

Escalation boundary - People track. Escalation. The single most important product-logic question is: at what point does a matter stop being safe for an SME to self-serve (with AI guidance, templates, checklists) and start requiring a human professional — consultant, employment lawyer, or registered HR practitioner? For "People" matters this boundary is reasonably well mapped by legal-commentary consensus: routine documentation, straightforward performance conversations and standard leave/entitlement questions are DIY-safe; anything involving termination with contested facts, discrimination, bullying/harassment complaints, restructures/redundancies, and enterprise agreements sits past the line.

Escalation boundary - Recruitment track. Escalation. On the hiring side, the escalation boundary is driven by a smaller number of high-complexity, high-consequence events rather than everyday volume: sponsoring a worker on a skilled visa, and — much more rarely for true SMEs — negotiating an enterprise agreement. Standard job ads, interviews and offers are DIY-safe; anything touching immigration law, industrial instrument-making, or a hiring decision that could be read as discriminatory is not.

Cost barrier - prohibitive/opaque legal fees. Economics. SMEs face genuinely high, and often opaque, professional fees for the exact moments they most need advice. Employment lawyers charge $220–$850+/hour depending on seniority (junior $150–$300+, mid-level $300–$500+, senior/specialist $500–$900+); HR consultants charge $150–$500/hour ad hoc or $1,500–$4,500/month on retainer. For a business with a handful of staff, a single complex termination or investigation can cost more in professional fees than the disputed entitlement itself.

Time poverty - admin crowding out the business. Economics. HR/compliance admin competes directly with the core job the SME owner or accidental HR rep was actually hired to do. Survey evidence consistently shows red tape, payroll compliance and HR/people issues ranking among the top time- and stress-drivers for small business leaders, ahead of many operational concerns.

Confidence barrier - "accidental HR" psychology. Psychology. People handling HR without an HR background or title — office managers, bookkeepers, operations leads, the owner themselves — report a persistent underlying anxiety that they will make a costly mistake without realising it, precisely because they don't know what they don't know. This is distinct from time poverty: it's a confidence/competence gap, not just a bandwidth one.

Where SMEs currently go for answers. Behaviour. In the absence of an affordable, reliable single channel, SMEs triangulate HR answers from a patchwork of free or informal sources of wildly varying quality: Google search, the Fair Work Ombudsman website and helpline, their bookkeeper or accountant, other business owners/"mates," franchisor guidance (for franchised operators), and industry association resources — with paid lawyer/consultant advice reserved for when a matter feels serious enough (see 6.5).

Economics of outsourced HR/legal advice (what's displaced). Economics. SMEs today pay for HR/employment-law reassurance through three broad channels: (1) hourly employment-lawyer engagement for specific matters, (2) HR consultant ad hoc hours or monthly retainers, and (3) fixed-fee outsourced HR/WHS subscription providers (the Employsure model) that bundle "unlimited advice" for a recurring fee. Each has a different cost/certainty trade-off, and none is well matched to a business that has no *constant* HR need but wants ongoing reassurance.
